Facts Expose Fallacies

ATISFIED THAT THE ECONOMIC POLICIES

of the Liberal government are. correct, Prime

Minister Pierre Trudeau admits he is puzzled by the cont#adiction of his theories by the facts.

. “Yes, I think it is a fair answer to say we are puzzled ... because every other economic indicator shows that the economy is booming,”-Mr: Trudeau

said.

If that were strictly true, how can it come about that so many Canadians still live below what is considered the poverty level?

How is it that national production lags and the rate of bankruptcy continues to increase?

Although the output of Canadian goods and services totalled $92.13 billion in 1971,,and the

$100 billion mark seemed likely in 1

, a large

part of the increase is discounted by inflation. Just how much, statisticians find it difficult to estimate. Moreover, the increase of the physical volume of output fell short of what the Economic Council of Canada has said the country needs to catch up with potential production and reduce urlemployment to

tolerable levels.

The 1971 gross national: production $92.13, the council estimates, fell about 2.4.per cent short of potential. In 1968 Canada was running only 1 per cent short of that goal.

Since Mr. Trudeau must be aware of these’ facts, and all his ministers with him, the perplexity of the government over continued unemployment increases and the failure of the unemployment in- surance formula cannot be accepted as sincere.

Bureau of statistics figures released from Ot- tawa on Wednesday disclose a significant reversal in trend. Instead of the consumer price index dip- ping in September, it climbed. Clothing and food prices led the way, the very items Canadian fami- lies can least afford to see advance.

THERE WAS A REPORTED CASE of bicycle 4. hit-and-run in Victoria the other day which, although not unheard of in the past, could serve a useful purpose now. It points to the continuing, in fact growing, popularity of cycling as a means of transportation for work as well as pleasure. And the incident might stir the authorities into paying greater attention to various factors involved.

There are many, and it would seem that the numbers of bicycles now on the streets call for con- trols that would be beneficial not only to unwary pedestrians but the pedal-pushers themselves.

The Bicycle Institute of America has come up with some startling statistics on bicycle sales in the United States which undoubtedly are corre- spondingly high in Canada, and which demand ac- tion. In 1960 sales south of the border amounted to 3.7 million. Last year they had boomed to 8.9 million. And by the end of this year it is estimated 11 million new bikes will have been purchased in

the 12 months.

With these increases is a rise in the number of bicycle thefts and ¢ycling injuries and deaths. The National Safety Council logged 850 deaths and 40,000 injuries in 1971 compared with 500 deaths

Martial Law a Dangerous Weapon

Marcos: Philippines’ Man in a Muddle

When martial law was final- ly imposed on the Philippines for the first time in the 26- year-old history of the in- dependent republic, President Ferdinand E. Marcos created both a shock and an anti- climax.

Martiallaw had long been expected as one possible out- come of the turbulent years of the Marcos presidency which began in 1965. Even during the calamitous floods which struck the Philippines in July and August this year, some Philippine commentators con- tinued their attack on martial law, and its suspected perpe- trator, the president.

For President Marcos, the floods carried a_ different meaning. Moving about the

countryside more freely than he has done in the last_two years, he saw that the dam- age done by the waters (some of which have not yet reced- ed) had set the economy, back by anything frou two’ to five years. And the economy was not doing particularly well be- fore the waters washed away crops and infrastructure.

Marcos is a man with a strong desire to give a greater sense of achievement and—direction-to a country whieh has generally followed an erratic course In the years since independence, never realizing its inherent promise. It-is-dikely.that~-he saw the floods as threatening to wash away his hoped-for place in future Philippine _ history books.

For this costly program Mr. Stanfield de- mands an accounting from the government. He is not alone. Most Canadians, aware that they face new taxes to support it, are anxious. By Special Correspondent from Hong Kong

Imelda Marcos continued to act-not only as a first lady should, but also as a future presidential candidate might.

‘The Constitutional Conven- tion, elected in 1970 to reform the democratic set-up in the country, accepted the parlia- mentary system instead of the present _ presidenti one. Marcos -had a great deal to do with that decision. So fears revived that his aim was to perpetuate his power as a prime minister.

* ek ok

Fears grew in September when the game convention majority defeated a resolution which, if passed, would have had the effect of preventing

either Mr. or “Mrs: “Marcos from running the country after the end of the pres-

ident's second term in 1973.

Last year, a. still unex- plained bombing at the na- tion's. forum for free speech, Plaza Miranda, had come close to decimating the Liber- ation opposition party leader- ship and resulted in Marcos suspending the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus.

The eventual withdrawal of the suspension under a furore of criticism was hailed-as a victory for civil rights and de- mocracy. The “victors”, how- ever, were not~~-seemingly reassured-~by—their- triumph and suspected that next time around, the president would opt for emergency power pro- vided by ‘the constitution. When a mysterious series of bombing incidents hit Manila in September, and when Marcos, without concrete, ob- jective evidence,-immediately blamed the communists, the “next time around’ seemed to be at hand.

Upder the Philippines cor

stitution, only “rebellion”, “insurrection” and = “ine vasion” are allowable pre- texts for martial law. So while Marcos could have made a gase for emergency powers b¥*citing the country’s endemic lawlessness, graft and corruption, he could not do so, constitutionally. So he declared martial law.

Marcos carefully brought all the wider evils and mal- practices of the republic into his justification of the deed, thereby obtaining a much greater degree of consent than if He had merely stuck to the communist menace. In proclaiming martial law, he also proclaimed a reforming zeal and "a new society.” The underlying message seemed to be: “Democracy got us into a terrible mess, I will see that martial law gets us out of it.”

The fact of importance now is that so many fell for it For, along with a widespread feeling that perhaps the pres- ident had done the right thing in the circumstances, went a sense of relief that the vio~ lence of Filipino politics had been stilled,

Defeat of Uruguayan Terror

Priorities

Mission

Accomplished Only at Great Cost

The Uruguyan govern- ment’s energetic onslaught against the Tupamaros has paid off handsomely — on the surface. About 2,400 urban guerrilla suspects are behind bars-and most of their known leaders have been slain or captured, including the found- er and leader Raul Sendie. He is now in hospital badly dis- figured by an army bullet that ripped through his cheeks.

More than 300 Tupamaro bolt-holes, including several “people’s prisons” and a well- equipped field hospital, have been discovered.

wk ok

The costs of this operation go far beyond the official fig- ure of $18 million spent by the armed forces and police in the last four years in the war against subversion. The cost may, indeed, be in- calculable, for the victory has also served, paradoxically, to weaken still further the rick- ety democracy the Tupa- maros had dedicated them- selves to destroying

While only mopping up operations remain for the sol- diers, their very success has increased the danger that the military will decide to pick up what remains of Uruguayan democracy. The general popu- lation is grateful that the ter- rorist menace has been, for the time being at least, crushed; but it is demoralized by the economic deterioration that has gone far beyond mere stagnation, the dilapida- tion of the cities and the lack of any clear vision in govern- ment circles of a way out of the mess.

In their battle with the ter- rorists the armed forces have absorbed some of their ene- mies’ ideas. The latest issue of Azul y Blanco (Blue ‘and White—the national colors) which is the mouthpiece of the more right-wing military establishment, whose repre- sentatives hold many of the key positions inthe armed forces, specifically stated that the armed forces did not see the suppression of the work- ing class as an integral part of their mission. The all-out war against terrorism has made the traditionally apoli- tical military chiefs more con- scious of the: plight of millions of ordinary Uruguayans,.and has reinforced their contempt for the civilian authorities. Azul y Blanco implied that the army had learned many lessons from its defeated foes, and was-not disposed to re- main a mere bulwark of a regime based on “‘social injus- tice.”

kok ok

The armed forces have quickly grown accustomed to playing a major role in Uru- guiayan. life,-and. have” given little indication that they are prepared to fade decorously from the scene now their duty has been accomplished.

The top brass is fascinated by thé example of the Peru- vian military dictatorship, which has been _ pushing through a number of populist: flavored social reforms against.the opposition of a rich elite that had controlled the country for generations General Gregoris Alvar, currently chief of Uruguay's joint generaly staff, is known to be attracted by this-line of thought.

The elected president, Juan Maria Bordaberry, a rich and conservative landownéf who assumed power on March 1 this year after a fiercely- fought election, \js well aware

By JAMES NEILSON from Buenos Aires

that the army is tempted to remain in the limelight and perhaps play an even bigger part in Uruguayan life. He is now studying a possible shake-up in the Uruguayan high command. The armed forces have made it clear that they would strongly resist this, and can persuasively point to the fact that they have eliminated Uruguay's toughest enemy and deserve to be treated with great resp- ect.

Although the Tupamaros have been physically beaten they had already achieved most of their short-term ob- jectives. Inflation is roaring through the Uruguayan econ- omy, plunging millions of Uruguayan workers into pen- ury and even resulting in cases of starvation in a country that, not so long ago. was overflowing with cheap fod. Bordaberry has commit. ted himself ‘to carrying through an extrengely strict austerity plan approved by the International Monetary Fund, and this has earned him the furious opposition of the trade unions which are de- manding a blanket wage rise of 40 per cent immediately. ‘They. Shave been harassing him with strikes that con- tinually bring the nation almost to a complete halt

Old democratic habits are

1 Beg to Differ

also in tatters: press cen- sorship is now part of the Uruguayan way of life and the government‘has even gone to the length of periodically banning such respectable, democratic Argentine news-

papers as La Prensa and Clarin. The “‘suspension of guarantees” which accom-

panied Bordaberry’s ‘‘state of internal war" allows arrested suspects to be held for as long as the police or armed forces desire, without the need to bring the prisoner before a magistrate. kok Ok

The inability of the com- mercial establishment or the politicians to cope with the crisis has eroded what faith the people had in them. Calls for even greater state inter- vention to prevent unemploy- ment following the bankrupt- cies of business concerns have been getting louder. The ar- gument that many of Uru- guay’s troubles can be laid at the fect of an already over-ex- tended state bureaucracy is all but ignored

The nation is also saddled with a huge foreign debt, which now reaches $750 mil- lion. Short-term debts needing rapid repayment total about $300 million this is. a country whose export earn- ings are stuck at $200 million a year.

In an effort to increase. ex. ports the government decided to institute a total ban on bect consumption, and this elimi- nation of what was once the staple diet of Uruguayans has increased discontent at all levels. It-has also encouraged the thriving black market, where prices are absurdly high for® the. housewives’ shrinking budgets.

As the disarray and help- lessness of the civilians be- comes more and more man- ifest, eyes are turning to the armed forces which are basking in the prestige gained by their defeat of the Tupa- maros. Their campaign was sometimes brutal and took in-

nocent lives, but it worked, and they showed efficiency The Tupamaros, after all,

were one of the most deeply- entrenched and best or- ganized guerrilla movements in the world. The armed forces, flushed with their suc- cess, have many officers who belicve they could be equally effective in solving the rest of the nation's problems.

Fears are growing that they could soon find an excuse to take over the government to rule in a nationalist, populist manner, with objectives that would be ironically similarsto those contained in what is known of the Tupamaros’ own ill—defined program for the or “after the revolu-

Extermination Either Way

Sometimes it seems to me that today the pendulum is swinging too quickly.

I mean, there was a day when we nursed the comfort- able theory that if the pendu- lum swung too far one way, in time it would swing the other way and so-give us some feel- ing of stability

But today the pendulum is swinging both ways at the same time.

The reason for this thought is that on my desk at the moment are two letters, from two well-known authorities.

One is a-lucid outline as to why man will have disap peared in a few hundred years because of the popula- tion explosion. In other words, we will have so many people we will eat our way out of the

only home we have the earth. This expert contends that

the only answer is ‘zero pop- ulation control’* that all families from now on should be limited to two children

The other expert writes, equally Tucidly, to explain that he believes man will dis- appear in the next few hundred years because of lack of population.

To merely maintain the numbers we have at present,

By FRANK LOWE

he tells me, each family should have a minimum of 24% children. The zero population theory means a steady decline and eventually disappearance

These two letters aptly illus- trate my dilemma. I'm essen- tially a quiet type who doesn't like arguments. But if I opt for the 2%4-child family I will be attacked by the two-child advocate, and vice versa.

The same holds true for most other questions plaguing me today. The ecology kick is @ good example.

For every learned article explaining to me how we are lousing up our world at a deadly rate, I would*see an- other one equally-as learned telling me the complete op- posite.

There are equally valid ex- amples. Save the seals, cries one group. If-thé seals are allowed to multiply, says an- other group, they'll eat all our fish

Wolves are good-bad. Tick off your-answer. Polar bears are on the increase-decrease. Do likewise. Socialism may be helpful-harmful to _ your wealth. Take your choice.

Today he is supposed to be an instant expert. As soon ax ecology was discovered a few years ago, for instance, ev- erybody had known about it all along:“fhey simply hadn't mentioned it before.

But within a day of its dis- covery radio commentators were commenting, writers were writing and TV panel shows were panelling

All of which made me feel rather inadequate. I mean how come those people knew so much so soon, while I knew nothing at all?

The same thing happened when somebody discovered that our oceans were ‘dying In a matter of hours people who had never ‘seen salt water were up to their mouths in the discussion — while I was still peering at an atlas trying to find out where that Humboldt Current really was.

It is all rather humiliating. So I have decided to swing with my very own pendulum.

The next time a new craze comes along, I ami going to studiously ignore it. No mat- ter what is written, said or shown about it, I will pretend it doesn’t exist.

When the chat at a cocktail party gets around to this lat- est fad or_newest popular di- saster, I'll firnily insist on talking about my theories as ty why Hindenburg lost the First World War.

Because I figure the newest popular disaster will either go away as suddenly as it ap- peared — or after about five years the hysteria will have been squeezed out of the sub- ject and a little rational dis- cussion can take place:

In other words, the pendu- lum will be swinging at its proper speed
